articles.title: Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims NHS Grampian patients unnecessarily bled to death
articles.summary: Dr Mohammed Habib said he had been raising concerns about NHS Grampian for a decade, including with government ministers and police.
articles.body:
A consultant surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary has called for a corporate homicide investigation into claims of avoidable deaths among NHS Grampian patients over many years.

Dr Mohammed Habib, who is still a surgeon at the hospital, said he had been raising concerns for a decade, including with government ministers and police, but he had been ignored.

The whistleblowing medic also leaked an unpublished expert review from 2022 which found 19 avoidable deaths among 45 patients in liver and pancreatic surgery, including some who bled to death in the operating theatre because of mistakes by surgeons.

The allegations come a week after a scathing report found poor leadership and culture at the NHS Grampian board. In response to the latest allegations, it said a thorough investigation had already taken place and any new evidence would be carefully considered.

John Swinney 'did nothing' about NHS Grampian concerns - party leaders

Habib, who has been a consultant with NHS Grampian since 2014, held a media conference on Thursday with his representative Aamer Anwar.

The lawyer and human rights campaigner said Habib had taken the step of speaking out because he was taught when he started as a doctor 36 years ago that taking care of patients must be his first concern.

Anwar said: "Catastrophically, the operating theatre he worked in at times could be described as a slaughterhouse, which killed through incompetence and negligence whilst not giving a damn for accountability."

Dr Habib said he was putting his career on the line to demand accountability from the health board over its failings.

The consultant said he formally reported serious concerns about dozens of avoidable deaths in 2021.

In 2024, he took 20 cases from the previous decade to the police but at the time no charges were brought.

Following Habib's news conference on Thursday, Detective Superintendent Carron McKellar confirmed that Police Scotland had received a report in 2024 "following several deaths".

He added: "Enquiries are being carried out, and a situational report will be submitted to the Procurator Fiscal."

A spokesperson for the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) said the concerns raised by the surgeon were "taken seriously".

They added: "Given the complexity and breadth of the issues raised, enquiries remain ongoing."

Whistleblower Habib had also leaked two reports by external experts which examined surgical care in NHS Grampian.

A 2022 review looked at 45 patients in the care of liver and pancreatic services at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI) between 2015 and 2021.

It said 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.

The 2022 review found that mortality rates for liver and pancreas surgery at NHS Grampian was very high.

It said that between 2017 and 2020 the overall death rate for major liver resections was 12% after 30 days and 18% after 90 days, compared to an expected rate of 2.2%.

The review criticised decision-making in liver surgery for occasionally being "overly aggressive", with surgery going ahead even if the disease was thought to be inoperable.

In pancreatic surgery, patients were regularly rushed into theatre without adequate planning or consideration of non-surgical alternatives, the experts said.

The review said blood losses in both surgeries was "unacceptably high" and said there was a lack of leadership and no clear standards for planning before operations.

It said poor decision-making and aggressive strategies were adopted despite high levels of deaths being predicted.

A second report earlier this year raised similar themes, with poor judgement about the risks and benefits of operating and repeated examples of massive blood losses and deaths during and after surgery.

It said it was clear that problems in the unit were "long standing and recurrent", adding that NHS Grampian had tried to improve outcomes but had not made the structural changes needed.

It noted that the unit did not have enough specialist staff to deliver the service safely, and that despite concerns being raised repeatedly since 2010, the issues had not been dealt with.

It strongly recommended that no complex or major HPB (Hepatopancreatobiliary) surgery should take place at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

Dr Habib, who has worked in General Surgery & HPB (liver, pancreas and bile duct) since 2014, said he thought several hundred patients had come to harm from an excessively high rate of complications.

He said he had tried his best to use the whistleblowing procedures but the institutions he had contacted had failed to act as robustly as they should have.

He said he first became aware of avoidable surgery-related deaths in 2016.

In July 2021, he formally raised serious concerns about what he believes were dozens of avoidable deaths.

In February 2024, he spoke to Police Scotland.

Habib said he believed NHS Grampian was guilty of "wicked recklessness and an indifference to patient deaths" and called for a corporate homicide investigation.

The consultant said the 2022 external expert report, which was never made public, concluded that 19 deaths out of a case study of 45 were avoidable (42%).

He said he had contacted the first minister and health secretary on numerous occasions since June 2023 but the Scottish government had said it had "no jurisdiction" to investigate whistleblowing claims.

Habib also said that the Independent Whistleblowing Officer (INWO) refused to progress his complaints.

He also wrote to the chief executive of NHS Grampian, Laura Skaife Knight, in December 2025.

She replied six months later saying she needed Healthcare Improvement Scotland to complete its enquiries.

In response to the latest allegations from Habib, Skaife-Knight said: "A thorough investigation has already taken place into these matters, with some elements of that work ongoing.

"Any new evidence or information will be carefully considered, and NHS Grampian will continue to respond through the appropriate clinical, governance and legal processes."

A Scottish government spokesperson said they recognised the "courage shown by this whistleblower" and reiterated that a "very significant level of intervention and an unprecedented level of support" was being given to NHS Grampian.

articles.title: Israeli shepherds report suspected 'agricultural terror' targeting livestock
articles.summary: An official source says dozens of animal poisoning cases have emerged in the West Bank, with contaminated cisterns and food bait found across grazing areas.
articles.body: A series of suspected animal poisonings has raised concerns among Israeli security officials, farmers and regional leaders about the growing threat to agricultural communities. Farmers say the attacks have resulted in significant livestock losses and warn that poisoned food and water sources could also endanger other animals and nearby residents. An Israeli source told Fox News Digital that military officials are taking reports of animal poisoning on Jewish-owned farms in the West Bank, known more commonly in Israel as Judea and Samaria, describing the incidents as "agricultural terror." The trend gained attention following an investigation by The Press Service of Israel (TPS-IL) that identified a cluster of poisoning incidents at farms across the Binyamin region over the past 12 months. CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND In a TPS-IL video, an Israeli farmer alleged that poisonings took place with substances placed within food such as dates and pita bread. "We have two populations with warm blood," the source said, referring to Israelis and Palestinians in the contested region. "Sometimes this manifests as verbal or physical violence, attacks, arson, property damage and, among other things, agricultural terrorism involving harm to animals." The source added that, "Lately, we have been receiving more and more reports of attempts by Palestinians to poison animals. We are talking about dozens of cases as we have seen in recent weeks … We act against terror. For instance, if we receive intelligence or information that a Palestinian intends to poison someone or has done so in the past, we will act to detain him, of course." The source advised farmers to remain in approved grazing areas, mark livestock as instructed and file a complaint for every incident to the relevant authorities, noting that animal poisoning is considered a cruel act. VANCE’S MIDTERM BLAME GAME HITS SNAG AS TRUMP’S OWN ISRAEL AMBASSADOR DISPUTES KEY CLAIM Evyatar Karo, one of the leaders of the farming movement whose Metzudat David farm is located in the Binyamin region north of Jerusalem, has been among the hardest hit by the poisonings. He told Fox News Digital that the incidents began in Nov. 2025. Karo said he went out to the pasture, as he did every day, and spotted one of his goats lying on the ground, gasping for air and drooling. He then saw another goat in the same condition. "Suddenly, we found dates scattered about — strange, because they weren't natural; they had a blue substance inside," he said. Karo said he mixed veterinary medication with water and administered it to the goats in an attempt to prevent the toxin from spreading through their bodies. One goat survived, but four died. "We brought in the Nature and Parks Authority to investigate the matter. The poison is lethal. If the carcass of an animal that died from this substance is left in the field, it poses a danger to other animals that might eat it. It works like a chain that can affect other wildlife," he told Fox News Digital. ISRAEL’S E1 PLAN EXPLAINED: THE JERUSALEM-AREA CORRIDOR SPARKING INTERNATIONAL BACKLASH Karo claimed that one of the poisons used was Lannate, a broad-spectrum carbamate insecticide commonly used by farmers, but said it was being deployed in highly concentrated form. "We lost 25 animals. It’s a terrible thing. The animals just die in your hands. They scream and cry. You can see them choking — it’s a horrible substance," he said. Karo said police had opened an investigation, but he feared the incidents could escalate. "It’s not just me, either — it involves a whole network, a lot of places. It occurred in Gush Etzion and Shiloh, including incidents involving poisoned water cisterns," he said. "We are speaking of organized Palestinian squads. They see where we take our animals and spread the poison there. It starts with animal lives, but eventually they can hurt people." TPS-IL recorded further suspected poisoning incidents in January and February 2026, followed by several additional cases. Among them were the discovery of contaminated water in approximately 10 cisterns near Alon Road, close to al-Mughayyir, on May 5; an incident at Shlisha Farm on June 7, in which two sheep were killed and around 15 others fell ill; and the discovery of poisoned food bait near Tel Talpiot, close to Gush Shiloh, in July. In the latter case, two guard dogs died within minutes, and a goat reportedly also died. But the Palestinians are also accusing the Israeli settlers of taking revenge against their livestock. The official Palestinian Authority news agency, WAFA, reported last Thursday that 13 sheep died, and several others suffered poisoning after an alleged attack by "Israeli colonists" west of al-Auja, north of Jericho. Sheep owner Suleiman Mleihat told WAFA that dozens of "Israeli settlers" sprayed toxic substances on an area where his flock was grazing. He added that a veterinarian had examined the animals and determined that poisoning caused the deaths. Mleihat said his sheep are kept on a farm on the outskirts of the area, which is frequented daily by local Israelis and security forces. While they are often grouped under the term "Hilltop Youth" — a label associated with individuals who establish outposts in volatile areas near Palestinian communities, sometimes leading to violent clashes — most residents of Judea and Samaria reject the name. Yisrael Ganz, governor of the Binyamin region and chairman of the Yesha Council, an umbrella organization representing Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria, warned that anyone willing to poison a goat could eventually target local residents. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "It could be a child tomorrow who sees the dates on the ground and eats them. Think about a shepherd who takes his children out into the area. If they’re able to poison our water sources, they could hurt thousands of people," Ganz told Fox News Digital. "They killed goats, dogs and cows, and we are sure we will be the next targets. It could happen today, with the same dates left near a playground or daycare. "The terrorists will have no more mercy for humans than they do for goats," he continued. "When someone kills goats to terrorize the shepherd, they can kill the shepherd, too. When someone says he wants to kill you and has found a way to do so, you have to worry that one day he will succeed. We don’t have to wait for that." Ganz cited 16 incidents but said the increasing frequency was his greatest concern. Recently, he said, incidents had occurred almost every week. "When they see that they are succeeding, they improve their techniques," he said. Ganz said dozens of body cameras funded by donors had been distributed to shepherds as an immediate response, but stressed that this could not replace action by the authorities. He said addressing the incidents was a top priority, warning that if poison reached water sources serving Jerusalem or other parts of Judea and Samaria, it could result in a major attack. Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) told Fox News Digital that the Civil Administration takes reports of suspected poisoning involving grazing areas, water sources or animals very seriously and works to investigate every case brought to its attention. Through its Agriculture Unit, the Civil Administration maintains ongoing cooperation and communication with relevant authorities and their professional counterparts to ensure a safe environment for animals in Judea and Samaria and address agricultural and animal-related needs. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Upon receiving a report, the unit's professional personnel conduct field inspections, collect findings and evidence, and, when necessary, take samples of the suspected substance and submit them for testing at specialized laboratories, including the Ministry of Agriculture's laboratories in Beit Dagan, in order to determine the circumstances of the incident and establish a professional assessment of the situation. Based on the findings and identified needs, the unit coordinates assistance, including the provision of medicines, food and water," COGAT said. "The potential effects of toxic substances on soil, water sources and the environment depend, among other factors, on the type of substance, its concentration and the characteristics of the affected area. Therefore, each case is assessed individually. The Civil Administration attaches great importance to environmental protection in Judea and Samaria and acts within its authority to identify and address environmental hazards," it added. COGAT emphasized that investigating these incidents and taking action against those responsible falls under the jurisdiction of the Israel Police. Fox News Digital contacted the Israel Police but did not receive a response before publication.

articles.body: An underwater world millions of years in the making is now at the centre of a growing battle between environmental protection and fossil fuel expansion. From Hollywood stars to celebrated Australian musicians and authors, more than 150 prominent figures are joining forces to prevent a major offshore gas development from transforming a remote marine sanctuary into an industrial site. With a crucial government decision still pending, the campaign to protect Scott Reef is gaining momentum, placing renewed attention on the potential consequences for Australia's extraordinary marine biodiversity.Hugh Jackman and Australian celebrities unite against gas drillingAccording to The Guardian and Greenpeace Organisation, more than 150 Australian artists, entertainers and creative professionals have signed an open letter urging Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt to reject Woodside Energy's proposed Browse gas development.The campaign includes internationally recognised actor Hugh Jackman, alongside Rebel Wilson, Simon Baker, Richard Roxburgh and Mia Wasikowska. The music industry is also strongly represented, with prominent names such as Kevin Parker of Tame Impala, Jessica Mauboy, Tina Arena, Paul Kelly, G Flip, Missy Higgins, Jimmy Barnes and Vance Joy supporting the initiative.Australian authors JM Coetzee, Helen Garner, Anna Funder, and Diana Reid have supported the appeal, demonstrating the growing involvement of the creative community in environmental advocacy. The campaign targets drilling up to 57 gas wells near Scott Reef, 270-300 kilometers off Western Australia's Kimberley coast, the report states.Scott Reef: Why it's an environmental flashpointScott Reef supports over 1,500 species, including endangered pygmy blue whales and vulnerable marine turtles.Greenpeace Organisation has warned that the proposed development could threaten important whale migration routes and expose marine ecosystems to the consequences of industrial drilling. The organisation also estimates that the Browse project could generate approximately 1.6 billion tonnes of climate pollution over its lifetime.The Guardian has reported that concerns extend beyond greenhouse gas emissions. Potential oil spills, underwater seismic activity and infrastructure development have raised questions about the long-term survival of the reef's fragile ecosystem. Greenpeace has also nominated Scott Reef for National Heritage listing, citing its exceptional ecological and scientific importance.Environmental concerns put Woodside's proposal under scrutinyWoodside Energy, which describes Browse as Australia's largest undeveloped offshore gas resource, first proposed the project in 2018. The development would involve transporting gas approximately 900 kilometres to the company's North West Shelf export facility. However, environmental assessments have raised concerns about the project's safeguards.According to The Guardian, Western Australia's independent Environmental Protection Authority previously criticised proposed measures to protect marine turtles and blue whales, warning that they could prove ineffective. A draft assessment also raised doubts about whether the risks associated with a potential oil spill could be reduced to an acceptable level.Woodside, however, has defended its proposal, maintaining that Scott Reef itself would not be drilled, mined or built upon. The company has also disputed descriptions of the development as an oil project, identifying it instead as a natural gas and condensate operation.Government decision could shape Scott Reef's futureThe federal assessment remains ongoing under Australia's Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, with the decision timeline paused while additional technical advice is considered, The Guardian reported.Meanwhile, Greenpeace campaigners are urging the Albanese government to reject the proposal, arguing that protecting Scott Reef would safeguard an irreplaceable natural environment for future generations. With more than 150 prominent Australians now backing the campaign, the debate surrounding Browse has become about more than an energy development. The pending decision could determine whether one of Australia's remarkable marine ecosystems remains protected from large-scale industrial expansion.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Historic trilateral summit: Trump, Xi & Putin sign 'Declaration Toward Peace', take 4 big pledges
articles.summary: Russia, China and the United States on Thursday adopted a joint declaration following a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, committing to reform the United
articles.body: Russia, China and the United States on Thursday adopted a joint declaration following a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, committing to reform the United Nations, increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products and hold discussions on reducing nuclear risks.The declaration, titled 'The Russia-China-US Heads of State Declaration Toward Peace', was adopted after US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen on November 19.According to the declaration, the three leaders held an in-depth exchange of views on the international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security. The Russian and US presidents also expressed appreciation to China for hosting the trilateral summit.UN reforms, energy security among key commitmentsThe declaration said Russia, China and the United States, as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, had committed to reforming the UN to enable it to respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.The three countries also agreed to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations, reaffirming the importance of stable energy flows.On legal matters, the leaders recognised the importance of the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials. They also agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.Three leaders agree to dialogue on nuclear risksThe declaration reaffirmed the position that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. It said the three countries would hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.During the trilateral meeting, Trump also described the three countries as being uniquely positioned to discuss reducing the number of nuclear weapons and lowering the risk of their use.“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used.”Xi described the summit as being of “groundbreaking significance”, while underlining the importance of cooperation among major powers in safeguarding global peace and stability.Putin said Russia, China and the United States could strengthen global stability through constructive cooperation.Also check: 'Chaos if major powers clash': Xi's warning at trilateral with Trump, Putin - who said what Trump, Xi and Putin hold trilateral summitThe trilateral meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit, lasted more than an hour.Opening the meeting, Trump said the three leaders would discuss “all problems that are being discussed in the world”, adding that all three countries had special responsibilities.Before the trilateral talks, Trump also held a separate bilateral meeting with Xi, marking their third substantial meeting this year.You use AI every day. articles.title: Woman who says abortion pills nearly killed her urges RFK Jr to act as group demands mail-order crackdown
articles.summary: Haile McAnally, who said she nearly died after taking abortion pills, says mailing mifepristone to doorsteps is reckless as she urges RFK Jr. to act.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A woman who said she nearly died after taking abortion pills is urging Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to crack down on mail-order access to the drugs, warning that shipping them directly to women's homes is "reckless" and could put more lives at risk. Haile McAnally, who said she suffered severe bleeding and required a blood transfusion after taking abortion pills 14 years ago, is speaking out in response to a Nov. 6 letter from Susan B. Anthony (SBA) Pro-Life America. The letter called on Kennedy to immediately restore in-person dispensing requirements for mifepristone while the Food and Drug Administration conducts a safety review. "Mailing them across the country to doorsteps just as easily as you could an Amazon package is not only reckless, it puts a lot of women's lives and safety at risk," McAnally told Fox News Digital. EX-DEMOCRAT SHARES ABORTION PILL EXPERIENCE THAT LEFT HER 'HEMORRHAGING IN THE BATH' McAnally, who serves as communications director for the Nebraska Republican Party and works with SBA Pro-Life America on legislation, recalled her harrowing experience that she previously shared with Fox News Digital in September. "I had my own run-in with abortion pills 14 years ago," McAnally said. "When I took these pills at a clinic and ended up having severe side effects, I wound up alone in my bathtub, almost dying from these pills, needing a blood transfusion at the hospital." The abortion pill mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain pregnancy, and is followed by misoprostol to complete the abortion process. An April 2025 study conducted by conservative think tank the Ethics and Public Policy Center found that 10.93% of women "experience sepsis, infection, hemorrhaging, or another serious adverse event within 45 days following a mifepristone abortion." In its letter, SBA argued that Kennedy has the legal authority to immediately suspend certain drug approvals if he determines they pose an imminent threat to public health. McAnally said she is imploring Kennedy to have greater oversight of the drug. FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS "I just continue to urge the federal government, especially RFK Jr. and the senators … to make sure that we really think about the ramifications of letting this go through so easily," she said. "I think we really need to put women first, women's safety first and not be so callous about this issue because it's going to be huge. Life is precious. Women's lives are precious, and women's safety deserves the utmost importance when it comes to this issue." The group points to a Justice Department filing earlier this year that it says confirms Kennedy could use that authority to reverse the Biden administration's 2023 changes allowing mifepristone to be dispensed by mail. The organization is urging Kennedy to reinstate the requirement that abortion pills be dispensed in person while the FDA completes its broader safety review of the drug. "Secretary Kennedy, you possess clear statutory authority to protect women from this growing form of abuse," the letter reads. "Federal law authorizes the HHS Secretary to suspend the approval of a drug application (including a supplemental application) ‘immediately’ if the Secretary ‘finds that there is an imminent hazard to the public health.’ In a legal brief filed earlier this year on behalf of HHS and FDA, the Department of Justice confirmed with the federal district court your legal authority to immediately suspend supplemental drug approvals — which would include the Biden FDA’s 2023 changes to the Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for mifepristone." TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER The Trump administration's reported decision to drop Heidi Overton's nomination adds complications to the debate over abortion pill regulations, as SBA presses Kennedy to act before the FDA completes its mifepristone safety review. Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at SBA Pro-Life America, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Now that the White House has pulled Heidi Overton’s nomination, we look forward to meeting with the administration’s new nominee for FDA Commissioner. We hope to secure two fundamental commitments on abortion-drug policy before the Senate proceeds with any confirmation vote." Baptist continued, "The administration must immediately end the Biden FDA’s mail-order abortion-drug scheme and protect pregnant women from predators who coerce or poison women with these drugs. And the FDA must fix its flawed safety study by obtaining robust data, increasing real-time transparency, and inviting external experts to help with this study." He added, "Confirmation is not a coronation. It is a time to vet nominees and seek commitments before they take office." WOMAN HELD DOWN, FORCE-FED ABORTION PILLS AT HEART OF ‘HELL ON EARTH’ FIGHT OVER BIDEN-ERA POLICY In the meantime, McAnally stressed the urgency of halting mail-order abortion pills while the FDA completes its safety review. "We're asking that we put a stop to these mail-order abortion drugs and not only for more research into mifepristone and the side effects, but just because the recklessness and the side effects that these have," McAnally said. articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: What is a dirty bomb? Explosive terror threat explained
articles.summary: Iran's reported dirty bomb exploration puts new focus on a threat experts say could shut down a city and displace families even without mass casualties.
articles.body: While no dirty bomb is known to have been successfully detonated in a terror attack, a reported Iranian effort to explore such an option has placed a new spotlight on long-standing fears of one — even as experts say the disruption could spread farther than the blast. A dirty bomb is an explosive designed to spread radioactive material — but not in the way an atomic bomb like those dropped in World War II would. "Anything involving radiation sounds frightening, but there’s a big difference between a dirty bomb and a nuclear weapon," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory special agent who at one point served as the Jackson Field Office's weapons of mass destruction coordinator. Dirty bombs use a conventional blast to spread radioactive dust or a similar contaminant. US REMOVES RADIOACTIVE CANCER-TREATMENT MATERIAL FROM CENTRAL AMERICAN COUNTRY OVER 'DIRTY BOMB' RISK "The initial blast may pose the greatest immediate danger, but the contamination, fear and disruption afterward could be significant," Pack told Fox News Digital. "A dirty bomb doesn’t have to kill thousands of people to terrorize millions." An attack could certainly be deadly. It would also shut down significant portions of a targeted city, he said, displacing families and businesses. They're also risky to build, according to Pack. Bomb makers are at risk of exposing themselves to the same radioactive material they plan on using against the public, it's difficult to ensure the contaminants are dispersed in the explosion, and the terrorist would need to procure something to disperse to begin with. "Just because somebody puts radioactive material with an explosive doesn’t mean they’re going to contaminate half a city," he said. "But even a relatively small incident could create tremendous fear, evacuations and disruption. That’s why we take these threats seriously." The radioactive materials to make them can be gathered without the ability to produce nuclear power or weapons, according to Paul Mauro, a retired NYPD inspector and Fox News contributor. One potential source is medical waste, he said, such as byproducts of certain cancer treatments. "That's why they call it dirty," he said. "It's waste." The greatest danger of a dirty bomb is the blast itself, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but radioactive material can spread and quietly cause dangerous health problems for people who unknowingly breathe it in. "The radioactive materials used in a dirty bomb would probably not create enough radiation exposure to cause immediate serious illness, except to people who are very close to the blast site," according to the CDC. Police departments are equipped with devices that can detect radiation, Mauro said — which are sensitive enough to flag medical radiation in a passing ambulance. IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS CNN reported earlier this week that U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing potential plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological device or chemical weapon, although sources described the effort as Iran exploring options rather than plotting an attack. The issue came up again at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing Wednesday morning involving testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia. IRGC OPERATIVE LANDS ON FBI’S MOST WANTED TERRORISTS LIST OVER ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL FORMER TRUMP ADVISOR Clayton acknowledged that the threat of a dirty bomb attack has existed for years, but officials said they haven't seen evidence of an imminent plot. "In the aftermath of September 11, 2001, there is heightened concern that terrorists may try to smuggle nuclear or radiological materials into the United States," the United States Government Accountability Office warned in a 2006 report. "These materials could be used to produce either an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, known as a dirty bomb." The GAO report cited a failed attack in Russia's capital in the mid-1990s as an example of the "capability and willingness" of terrorists to resort to such weapons of mass destruction. Chechen separatists had placed a canister packed with cesium-137 and dynamite in a Moscow park, but it wasn't detonated. The report included a summary of Department of Energy plans in place to scan for and detect sources of radiation that could be linked to terror plots or weapons smuggling and even locate material washed away in the wake of a natural disaster like Hurricane Katrina. Now, the source of potential threats is believed to be Iran or its proxy militia group, Hezbollah. "The best dirty bomb response is the one that you never hear about," said Pack, the retired FBI agent. "Because somebody stopped the plot before a bomb ever made it onto our streets." SEND US A TIP Radiation has no taste or smell, according to the CDC. If you find yourself in the midst of a suspected dirty bomb attack, the CDC warns that you should cover your mouth and nose and try not to breathe it in. If you aren't already indoors, seek shelter. Remove your clothes and seal them in a bag, then shower up, making sure to thoroughly wash your hair to remove any potential contaminants. Indoors, close doors and windows and turn off fans that bring in outside air. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Monitor TV, radio or social media for official updates. Authorities will announce when it's safe to go outside again. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "The good news is that it can be cleaned up," Mauro said of the dispersed material. "It would be expensive, time-consuming, a nightmare, sure." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Krista Garvin and Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.title: Viagogo may have broken law on hidden fees, watchdog provisionally finds
articles.summary: The UK's competition body says initial findings suggest the ticket-reselling website used drip pricing.
articles.body:
Ticket-reselling site Viagogo may have broken the law on hidden fees, the UK's competition body has said in a provisional finding.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it found that Viagogo failed to show consumers the total price upfront when they were buying tickets "and added fees later in the process, a practice known as drip pricing".

The CMA added that this was an initial finding, and it should not be assumed that the company had actually broken the law.

In a statement, Viagogo said it was co-operating fully with the CMA, adding that the investigation was continuing and "no final findings have been made".

The CMA said last year that it was investigating a number of companies over their online pricing practices, including Viagogo.

The competition watchdog said it had looked into the experience of UK fans buying tickets for events such as concerts and sport on three websites that operate under the Viagogo brand.

"The CMA believes that mandatory costs such as taxes and booking fees were added at later stages of the checkout process and not included in the total price from the start," it said.

"Drip pricing can cause fans to be caught out by extra charges and buy tickets they might not otherwise have selected, had they been able to compare prices accurately from the start."

The CMA said Viagogo would now have an opportunity to consider its findings and respond before a final decision is made.

"This is an ongoing investigation and no final findings have been made," Viagogo said in a statement.

"We have engaged constructively with the CMA and continue to cooperate fully with its investigation."

The CMA has powers to tackle anti-competitive behaviour. It can now decide if consumer laws have been broken - rather than having to go through the courts.

Drip pricing is one of the practices the CMA has been focusing on particularly.

On Wednesday, it said it was investigating three companies over the issue, and in August it announced that the Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School had been engaged in the practice.

In general, the CMA can impose penalties of up to 10% of global turnover for a breach of consumer law. However, it will consider a number of factors, including the severity of conduct, before deciding on the size of the penalty.

In June this year, the watchdog ordered rival ticket reseller StubHub UK to refund more than 50,000 customers and pay a £900,000 fine for not showing people the total price upfront when buying tickets.

StubHub UK received a 40% reduction to its financial penalty after it admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early with the CMA.

articles.title: Florida set to carry out its record-breaking 20th execution same day as a Texas lethal injection
articles.summary: Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to execute a man convicted of killing a Houston jeweler during a $3.6-million diamond robbery.
articles.body: Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to execute a man convicted of killing a Houston jeweler during a $3.6-million diamond robbery. Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, is scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison in Raiford. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, is set to receive a lethal injection an hour later at a prison in Texas and become the ninth person executed by that state this year. The planned executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the aging of the U.S. death row population. Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his office on Jan. 24, 1996. Florida has carried out more than half of the nation’s 37 executions this year under outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. Thursday’s scheduled executions come amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the United States following Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in October. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty’s reinstatement in 1976. Thursday’s execution would surpass the 2025 total, with two more Florida executions scheduled in December. Appeals in the cases in Texas and Florida were pending. Autopsies found Florida husband and wife were strangled The MacIvors were found dead in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, according to court records. Autopsies determined both had been strangled and that Susan MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner also said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death. Investigators collected DNA evidence from the scene, but initially found no match with any samples in the state’s database. But then Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996. Authorities said a sample taken from him matched the sample collected at the MacIvors’ home, and he was charged with their killings. Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each. Defense attorneys had argued that investigators had planted the DNA evidence. Diamonds missing in jeweler’s killing were never recovered Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes had arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours. According to court records, she opened the door for him and his brother the night of the shooting and also distracted the security guard at Dennes’ request. The guard, who was shot twice but recovered, identified Dennes as his disguised attacker. Later that evening, police were called to the building and found the jeweler’s body upon entering his office, according to court filings. The documents said officers found the jeweler’s safe was empty with no signs of the diamonds or the $200,000 in cash he was supposed to have on hand. The diamonds have never been recovered. Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove that he killed Szucs. Prosecutors noted in a recent court filing that Dennes, who came to the U.S. from Cuba with his family as a child, admitted guilt during a Spanish-language interview with Telemundo in 2022. “I did those things, so I am guilty,” Dennes told Telemundo, adding that he regretted taking a man’s life, the prosecutor’s filing said. A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
articles.summary: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.

In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.

While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".

Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance

This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls

The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.

Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".

Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.

Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.

"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."

Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".

It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."

"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".

Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.

He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".

Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".

He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.

As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.

Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.

In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.

There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.

The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.

"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.

"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."

The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.

"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."

Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.

It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".

Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.

Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.

The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.

US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.

"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.

But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".

"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.

"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."

Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.

"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.

With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

articles.title: Baby marmoset rescued from shed finds new mum at Monkey World
articles.summary: Gino, five months old, was at risk of hypothermia and has now been adopted by another marmoset.
articles.body:
A baby marmoset that was kept in a dirty birdcage with only a lamp for warmth has been given a new home after being rescued by police.

Gino, thought to be five months old, had been taken from his family to be sold as a pet and was being held in a garden shed in south London.

Metropolitan Police officers found him at risk of dying of hypothermia when they went to the address, and removed him with help from Monkey World in Dorset.

Gino, who was named after one of the officers who led the rescue, is now recovering at the centre, where he has been adopted by Minty, an adult female marmoset.

Det Con Gino Ferrara said: "When I saw the marmoset I was shocked. The yard where he was being kept smelt awful, like faeces, and there were dogs running loose and barking constantly.

"You could hear this little monkey screaming. We could just tell he was scared. He looked shocked and confused."

Dr Alison Cronin, director of Monkey World, who helped with the rescue, said: "I was surprised that baby Gino was still alive, as he is so young and was left on his own in a cold garden shed in a bird cage.

"It must have been lonely, scary, and very cold, especially for a youngster who should still be carried by his parents."

At five months old, marmosets would normally still be riding on their parents' backs and feeding on their mother's milk.

Gino weighed just 140g when he was found. His poor diet and living conditions have left him with early signs of rickets, which weakens bones.

Staff said they hope he was found in time to make a full recovery.

Cronin said: "We are so pleased for Gino that he has found a mum in Minty and that he is now getting the specialist care that he needs."

Gino is the 100th marmoset the centre has taken in from the UK pet trade, out of 153 primates in total.

England has brought in licensing rules for keeping primates as pets, but Scotland and Wales have no equivalent.

Monkey World has started a petition calling for similar laws in Wales.

articles.body: A homeowner’s lucrative rental property investment within an affluent Pacific Northwest community was allegedly hijacked by the very property manager he hired, sparking a months-long squatter standoff that ended with a $1 deed, a shooting on the property and the manager behind bars. Ellis Cameron shared his story with Fox News Digital and says he hired Junior Patrick Adelbai to manage property he purchased and renovated in Edgewood, Washington. Instead of managing the rental, the homeowner said the alleged squatter decided to move his family in, causing a months-long legal battle for the homeowner and making him unable to sell it. The homeowner intended to have Adelbai rent out the property for $6,500 a month. After the pair reached an agreement, Cameron changed the locks to prep it for renters. The homeowner said Adelbai moved his family in and lived in the house without running water for nearly two months – and made a mess of the inside and outside of the property, as depicted in a series of photos he shared with Fox News Digital. NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE' Cameron said he was left paying the mortgage without the rental income he was anticipating to cover the payments. He asked the family to leave on numerous occasions, enlisting the help of law enforcement at times, but was told the dispute was a "civil matter" that would have to be resolved through the court system. 'TOXIC COCKTAIL' OF RENTER PROTECTIONS DESTROYED $39M AFFORDABLE HOUSING INVESTMENT AS DEM CITIES FOLLOW SUIT "You have squatter-friendly laws that protect the squatters," Cameron said. "In Washington state, especially Pierce County, it's a high-risk agreement to decide to rent your place out because if something doesn't go right, it's going to be problematic for you. In Washington state, you can't turn off the squatters' utilities, you can't threaten them." ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS State law says landlords cannot evict tenants on their own. Instead, they must notify law enforcement, give proper notice and let courts handle the removal. SEND US A TIP LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Making matters worse, the homeowner said Adelbai's wife weaponized law enforcement against him when he tried to show the home in hopes of selling it. "She held my place sabotaged for months because the law protected her," he said. HOMEOWNERS TERRORIZED BY PRO SQUATTERS TURNING DREAMS INTO NIGHTMARES IN PALM-LINED PARADISE, EXPERTS SAY Cameron went on to say, "I had a real estate agent [give] a 48-hour notice to the squatter, and she called the police when [the agent] showed up and [she told police] she didn't want to show the place." The situation reached a breaking point when Adelbai allegedly shot at someone on the property in March, claiming self-defense while simultaneously claiming he was the homeowner, Cameron said. The situation escalated March 19, when records show a quitclaim deed prepared and signed by Adelbai was filed with the Pierce County Auditor’s Office, KIRO7 reported. Adelbai claimed he owned the property in the document and transferred ownership to his wife, Karmaleen Issac, for $1. "Title fraud is devastating, and the law needs to change. More protection is needed in Washington state and nationwide," Pierce County Auditor Linda Farmer said. In the interim, Pierce County has launched a free "Owner Alert" service, which notifies homeowners of suspicious filings so they can take rapid legal action. Over 7,000 residents have already signed up. Meanwhile, Adelbai is currently in jail with a list of pending charges. The Pierce County Sheriff's Office confirmed the suspect's arrest to Fox News Digital, but did not provide details into the incident or shooting. articles.title: H-1B-hater Bo French expelled from an exclusive club for his racist remarks. He says he didn't make any offensive comment; 'Members have slept with others' spouses. Have you asked them to resign?'
articles.summary: Texas Republican Bo French was dealt a second blow after his crushing defeat in the state's Railroad Commission election after an exclusive club expelled
articles.body: Texas Republican Bo French was dealt a second blow after his crushing defeat in the state's Railroad Commission election after an exclusive club expelled him for his anti-immigration and racist remarks. Politico reported the expulsion and added that in its November 10 letter, the River Crest Country Club informed French that the board of directors voted to terminate French's membership immediately “for reasons relating to the reputation and general welfare of the Club.”River Crest Country Club, founded in 1911, is one of Fort Worth's oldest and most prestigious private clubs. It reportedly charges a $75,000 initiation fee and monthly dues of around $800.“There is a cost to fighting for what is right,” French wrote on X on November 19, sharing his account of the expulsion and the statement he presented to the board.French said the club had first asked him to resign in September over what it described as his “racist posts”. He refused, prompting the board to convene an expulsion meeting, where members ultimately voted to remove him.In his six-page defence, French made an emotional appeal to the board, highlighting his family's decades-long association with the club.“I have been a member here for 30 years. Longer than I think all of you,” he told the board, adding that both his brothers and his mother were also members. He said his family had been associated with the club since it opened 115 years ago and that he, along with his children, loved the establishment. French also accused the club of applying double standards, claiming that he had witnessed other members making racist remarks towards minority members without facing similar consequences.“I have witnessed many members saying very racist things to minority members... I am just curious, have you asked any of those members to resign?” he asked. He also said that members have slept with others' spouses and asked whether those members had been asked to resign.He also alleged that Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick had played a role in the chain of events that eventually led to his removal from the club. French claimed Patrick had seized an opportunity to target him after an article about his controversial remarks circulated.What was the original controversy?The controversy surrounding French intensified in September when he posted a photograph of South Asian students celebrating the University of Texas at Austin's football victory over Ohio State. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” he wrote alongside the photograph.The post triggered accusations of racism, including from members of his own Republican Party. French, however, defended his remarks as criticism of university admission and hiring policies, insisting that he wanted institutions to prioritise Texans over foreign nationals.“It's not racist to point out that we should be favoring Texans over foreigners,” he said in a previous defence of his position.His anti-immigration campaign also became a major point of contention during his unsuccessful bid for the Texas Railroad Commission. French lost the November 3 election to Democrat Jon Rosenthal by approximately 677,000 votes.On H-1BIn his defense letter, French argued that the H-1B visa program is rife with fraud despite the good intentions with which the program was created. "90% of some groups have obtained these visas with fraudulent documents. Many visa holders immediately obtain additional visas to bring in their family and friends. These foreigners suddenly reap the benefits that should be reserved for citizens," he said, adding that the University of Texas counts both illegal aliens and scammers as Texans.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fiona Harvey, who allegedly inspired Baby Reindeer, to appear at Crown Court on harassment charge
articles.summary: Harvey, who allegedly inspired Netflix's Baby Reindeer, racially aggravated harassment without violence.
articles.body:
A woman who allegedly inspired the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix drama Baby Reindeer is to appear at Harrow Crown Court on charges of racially aggravated harassment without violence.

Fiona Harvey, 61, is accused of sending several emails and three voicemails including antisemitic material to lawyer Mark Lewis, between 4 September and 9 October 2025.

During a hearing at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday, the court heard that Lewis initially believed Harvey was a potential client.

Harvey of Camden, north London, did not indicate a plea, but elected for a Crown Court trial.

The charge is an either-way offence, which means it can be heard in either a magistrates' court or Crown Court.

She will next appear at Harrow Crown Court for a pre-trial preparation hearing on 17 December.

Harvey has previously identified herself as the woman on whom Martha is based, after the release of Richard Gadd's Emmy Award-winning series in 2024.

She is suing the streamer £128m for defamation, negligence and privacy violations, arguing that that Netflix told "brutal lies" about her to over 50 million viewers around the world.

Netflix denies the claim, which will be heard in front of a jury on May 18, 2027, at the US District Court for the Central District of California.

articles.title: EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10
articles.summary: The EU and UK are expected to reach new deals on food trade and visas for young people at a summit on Friday.
articles.body:
Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said.

The summit is aimed at reaching new agreements between the two sides on food trade rules, visas for young people and carbon emissions pricing.

The prime minister's spokesman said that if a deal is secured, the government will introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions and debates" of the Brexit referendum.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but added "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Burnham's spokesman said Brexit had done "more harm than good".

"The choice over the coming days is clear: stand with Boris Johnson and Kemi Badenoch defending a broken status quo, or with Andy Burnham delivering change, cutting costs for business, helping with the costs of the weekly shop and creating opportunities for young people," he added.

One of the deals expected to be reached on Friday includes a new youth mobility scheme, which would make it easier for young people to work and travel in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in the talks, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

An agreement on trade could also remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

On immigration, Burnham has said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from the deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

The prime minister has said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

articles.title: Somalia expels UAE ambassador, accuses Abu Dhabi of violating sovereignty
articles.summary: Somalia says the UAE is interfering in its internal affairs with actions that amount to an ‘open invasion’.
articles.body:
Somalia has ordered the United Arab Emirates (UAE) ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and withdrew its envoy from Abu Dhabi.

Announcing the measures on Thursday, Somali officials accused the UAE of violations of Somalia’s sovereignty that amounted to an “open invasion”.

“Measures will be taken against ‌anyone who cooperates with UAE in the invasion against Somalia,” Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud said in a broadcast on the state-run news agency.

According to the Somalia National News Agency, Mohamud said Abu Dhabi signed agreements related to the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo with regional administrations and without the Federal Government.

He also said that the UAE helped to establish military bases and forces outside Somalia’s national command while the army is fighting the al-Shabab armed group and had given political and financial support that fuelled disputes inside the country.

Expelling the UAE ambassador is the strongest measure Mogadishu has taken against Abu Dhabi since it annulled every agreement with the gulf state earlier this year.

The UAE has long leveraged its wealth to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, using a mix of economic, military and diplomatic clout to assert ⁠regional power.

articles.title: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.summary: Philip Young, 50, drugged and raped his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period.
articles.body:
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.

"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.

"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."

She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.

"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."

She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".

She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".

Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.

She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.

The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.

Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.

How Joanne Young was drugged by husband and raped by strangers over 13 years

The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".

One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.

As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.

Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.

James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."

The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.

Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.

Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.

The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.

Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.

They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".

Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.

"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."
