articles.title: Syria's Christian leaders warn of 'grave' threat to community's future amid wave of attacks
articles.summary: Syria's top Christian leaders warn that escalating attacks, kidnappings and violence threaten their community's future, as the State Department voices concern over religious persecution.
articles.body: The leaders of Syria’s oldest Christian denominations issued a dire warning about the intensified persecution of their communities and whether there is a future for them in the Middle Eastern nation. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former U.S.-designated terrorist who commanded the al Qaeda-linked Nusra Front during the nation's civil war, has since sought to distance himself from his extremist past as he oversees the nation's rebuilding amid a deteriorating situation for Christians and other minorities. Senior Christians released a joint statement that noted "a series of heinous and recurring attacks targeting the Syrian people, and Christians in particular. Time and again, we have raised our voices, and we continue to do so, as this wave of attacks has persisted without interruption. These attacks are not, and have never been, isolated incidents." The signers were John X, Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch and All the East, Ignatius Aphrem II, Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch and All the East, and Youssef Absi, Melkite Greek Catholic Patriarch of Antioch and All the East. SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE The religious leaders cited examples of recent violent attacks on members of the Christian community in the Muslim-majority country. "What has happened, and continues to happen, in many places, including most recently in Al- Suqaylabiyah, in the form of systematic assaults and kidnappings carried out for exorbitant ransom payments, constitutes a violation of the most basic human rights, as evidenced by the video showing the brutal torture of the jeweler Maher Sankari," they wrote. "In view of the competent authorities' failure to provide security and protection in response to what has occurred and continues to occur, these attacks have once again escalated in recent days, culminating in the targeting of Archbishop Youhanna Abdo Arbash of the Melkite Greek Catholic Archdiocese of Homs, Hama, Al-Nabk Yabroud, and their Dependencies. He was bound, blindfolded, and gagged while his office was ransacked. " The leaders warned about a "grave question regarding the future of Christians in this country." TURKEY DEPORTS PEACEFUL CHRISTIANS UNDER GUISE OF 'NATIONAL SECURITY' CLAIMS WATCHDOG A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "We are concerned by reports of attacks, kidnappings and violence against Christians in Syria and regularly raise these concerns with the Syrian government. We continue to stress the importance of protecting the unalienable rights of all Syrians, regardless of ethnicity or religion." Alberto Fernandez, former U.S. ambassador and Mideast analyst, who closely follows the persecution of Christians in the region, told Fox News Digital, "The government in Damascus is an Islamist-controlled one but has tried generally to treat Christians fairly — more so than the treatment of Alawites and Druze. So some Christian property has been returned and some Christian representation has been secured. The regime is still deeply ideological, and includes figures that are more extreme than the norm. " He added, "Christian existence is seen more as a concession than a question of fundamental rights. But the biggest danger for Christians has been the government's inability to secure law and order in the country, especially in some areas like Homs, and the difficulty in improving the country's disastrous economic situation. So deep economic crisis and crime/chaos have driven Christian flight more than actual persecution by the state. " Fox News Digital reported last year about radical Islamists who targeted Syrian Christians and reportedly murdered Khaled Mazhar, pastor of the Good Shepherd Evangelical Church in Sweida, along with 11 family members. An additional person survived the massacre of Christians because the Islamists thought she was dead. CHRISTIAN-JEWISH ORGANIZATION DELIVERS EMERGENCY AID TO PERCECUTED SYRIAN MINORITIES UNDER THREAT Syrian government actions While the Syrian government did not respond to Fox News Digital requests for comment, there have been some positive pronouncements over the last year, according to reports. After the bombing of the Mar Elias Church in Damascus last year, when the Islamic State murdered 25 people, President al-Sharaa pledged to tackle security threats against Christians. In 2025, his government said it prevented a planned attack on a church in Tartus. Syria’s Interior Ministry said two men had been arrested "en route to carry out a terrorist operation." Syria appointed Hind Kabawat, a lawyer, as minister of social affairs and labor. She is the only Christian and woman in the president's cabinet. A British government report from earlier this year seemed to downplay threats to the Christian community. It noted, in part, "Since coming to power in Dec. 2024, the new government has engaged with Christian and Shia community leaders and has provided security for religious sites and festivals. While there are reports of attacks, harassment and discrimination by both state and non-state actors, the frequency and severity of these incidents do not suggest that there is a generalized risk to Christians and Shia Muslims." Yet the Rev. Dr. Petra Heltd, a Christian scholar, told Fox News Digital, "The Joint Statement issued regarding the escalating wave of violence, extortion, and targeted attacks against the Christian communities in Syria is a heartfelt cry for help. " She said, "While standing in solidarity with the suffering brothers and sisters in Syria, we call upon international governments, diplomatic missions and multilateral bodies to take concrete steps to support and protect Christians in Syria and to speak out against those acts against the ancient, living Christian presence in the region — a community that has already dwindled from only roughly one million before 2011 to fewer than 300,000 today." We have already seen the consequences for the Druze and Alawites. This is a recurring pattern that should alarm everyone." He added, "The international community must stop mistaking promises of moderation for actual moderation. articles.title: In 2023, Australia installed 13 sculptures beneath Busselton Jetty to add marine habitat; divers reported nearly 20 species using them within weeks
articles.summary: Discover how Australia’s innovative underwater sculptures have transformed Busselton Jetty into a vibrant marine habitat, attracting nearly 20 species in just weeks.
articles.body: In 2023, a curious piece of art was created beneath the waters off Western Australia for a very different reason. 13 sculptures below the Busselton Jetty were attracting marine life within hours of being installed. Within weeks, divers reported that 20 species of animals moved in and were using the structure as a kind of home. However, at the end of the day, the artists creating them weren’t simply installing a public art project, but a piece of marine habitat creation.Thirteen sculptures transform the seabed into an artificial reefAccording to information from the Busselton Jetty, on Western Australia's south-west coast, it juts out into Geographe Bay and is the longest timber-piled jetty in the Southern Hemisphere. A colourful variety of marine creatures now inhabit what is today its wooden and steel piles. In 2023, the jetty’s environmental team amplified the miniature oceans by installing 13 sculptures made by artists from Western Australia. The sculptures included about 10 bronze mermaids, ceramic people and a 10 m-long steel whale, along with ceramic sculptures that each weighed about a tonne.The structures were placed beneath the sea near the end of the jetty, where they could serve as additional surfaces for marine organisms to colonise. Their location was particularly relevant because much of Geographe Bay's seabed consists of seagrass meadows, making suitable hard surfaces comparatively limited. According to the Busselton Jetty's environmental information, the existing reef beneath the structure supports more than 300 marine species. The sculptures were designed to extend this habitat by introducing additional solid surfaces and spaces into the surrounding marine environment.Marine creatures began exploring the artworks within hoursMarine life was drawn to the artwork soon after it was installed in the water. An ABC News story published on July 12, 2023, said a large school of skipjack tuna was recorded just hours after the first artwork went into the water and preferred one ship sculpture in particular over the following week. The Marine visitors became more diverse as further sculptures went into the water, with nearly 20 different species using the sculpture as habitat. Jetty environment manager Sophie Teede said.The ceramic work Postmaster General demonstrated the potential impact of design choices. Artist Georgia Zoric's 3 m-tall sculpture was built around stone water bottles with openings at its base, designed to offer refuge to octopuses, cuttlefish, eels and small fish. The swift response from marine life revealed the potential for underwater structures to provide new spaces for exploration and occupancy.A growing reef brings opportunities and ecological questionsThe project provided a pathway to linking marine conservation and engagement. Over time, the sculptures would have been colonised by marine life, with algae and other organisms growing on the surface and in crevices. Some areas would have formed hiding places for animals and would have ultimately become part of the oceanic environment. Visitors would have viewed these sculpture elements with the added richness of experience of the natural environment.The ecological benefits of artificial reefs rely on more than the quantity of fish they attract; the structural intricacy, location and ultimate impact on the neighbouring environment all contribute to the performance of these reefs. A 2024 study in Nature Sustainability reviews 109 studies and points to potential ecological benefits of artificial marine structures, varying by habitat type, species and structure. Ensuring the structures are not just for tourist attraction, the jetty’s environmental team will continue to keep an eye on how the structures evolve and form new habitats. While initial popularity and attraction to marine life progress, the long-term ecological impact remains.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Rival Bangladeshi party supporters fight on streets of London
articles.summary: LONDON: Violent street battles erupted between supporters of rival Bangladeshi political parties, the Awami League and the National Citizen Party (NCP),
articles.body: LONDON: Violent street battles erupted between supporters of rival Bangladeshi political parties, the Awami League and the National Citizen Party (NCP), in East London on Monday night.Dozens of Bangladeshi-origin men hit each other with long rods and tree branches and hurled wheelie bins, glass, pieces of concrete, eggs and traffic cones at each other in residential streets after an Awami League protest against NCP convener and opposition chief whip Nahid Islam outside the Mayfair Venue in Romford descended into violence.Police were called at 10 pm and the group dispersed shortly afterwards. Two ambulance crews treated six patients at the scene and took one to hospital. A police investigation is ongoing but there have been no arrests yet.Islam is in the UK on a week-long tour meeting UK supporters of his party, which, in an electoral alliance with Jamaat-e-Islami, won six seats in the Feb 2026 Bangladesh parliamentary elections. He was a ringleader of the July 2024 Students Against Discrimination movement which ousted Sheikh Hasina as PM.Dhaka’s foreign ministry on Tuesday strongly condemned the “violent, terrorist acts”, blaming them on “groups linked to the ousted ruling party” and called on the UK authorities to bring the perpetrators to justice.“Fugitive and extremist activists of the fascist Awami League attacked ordinary Bangladeshi expatriates and university students,” Islam wrote on X. “The Awami League’s activities are banned in Bangladesh under the Anti-Terrorism Act. In keeping with that violent past, it is now organising abroad to intimidate diaspora communities.”An Awami League Bangladeshi-origin supporter in London told TOI: “They have killed people, carried out arson and are involved with political persecution, so those people who have suffered or have relatives in Bangladesh went there to protest and raised peaceful slogans outside the hall.” He said the protest was peaceful until private security hired by NCP hit one of the Awami League supporters and said one Awami League supporter was taken to hospital with a serious head injury.Local MP Jas Athwal described the violence as “utterly unacceptable”. Tory MP Katie Lam said, “If you come to this country, you must leave foreign feuds behind”, while far-right party Restore Britain chief and MP Rupert Lowe said: “Deport the lot.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Priscilla Chan bought a $170 million Miami mansion on Billionaire Bunker Island, featuring a secret-passage library, a 1,500-gallon aquarium, 11 bathrooms and a private waterfront dock
articles.summary: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan have added another substantial property to their real estate portfolio with the purchase of a $170 million mansion on
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan have added another substantial property to their real estate portfolio with the purchase of a $170 million mansion on Indian Creek Island in Miami, Florida, an exclusive residential enclave often known as the ‘Billionaire Bunker’. Reported in March 2026, the transaction involved an unfinished property whose planned features set it apart from a conventional luxury residence. These include a library with a concealed passageway, a 1,500-gallon aquarium, a private dock and a swimming pool with approximately 30,000 square feet, designed to have nine bedrooms and 11 bathrooms once construction is complete.Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan's $170 million home on Miami's billionaire islandAs reported by the Wall Street Journal, Zuckerberg and Chan completed the transaction, acquiring the property for $170 million. The deal set a new residential property sale record for Miami-Dade County. The mansion stands on Indian Creek Island, a gated community situated in Biscayne Bay. The island covers nearly 300 acres and has around 41 waterfront residential plots. Its privacy, restricted access and high-value properties have made it a preferred address among wealthy business figures and celebrities.Reportedly, the couple's purchase places them among the residents of an area already associated with prominent names.What makes Zuckerberg and Chan's $170 million mansion stand outAlthough construction has not been completed, the plans offer a picture of what the finished residence will contain. The approximately 30,000-square-foot mansion is designed with nine bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, alongside several dedicated spaces for leisure and entertainment.One of its more unusual features is a library that will include a secret passageway. The property is also expected to have a 1,500-gallon aquarium, a party room, a gym, a hair salon and a separate massage room, as reported.These facilities are part of a wider design that gives considerable space to private recreation. Rather than simply providing additional bedrooms and living areas, the plans include rooms intended for different activities within the house itself.Private pool, garden and 200 feet of waterfrontThe outdoor arrangements are also extensive. The estate is expected to include a heated swimming pool, landscaped garden and private dock with direct water access. It has approximately 200 feet of waterfront, giving the property its own stretch along the island's coastline.The combination of a private dock and waterfront location is particularly relevant to Indian Creek, where many residences are built around access to Biscayne Bay. The gated community also has its own police force and a golf course, adding to its appeal as a private residential destination.The mansion's construction and design have been underway for several years, with the current owners having acquired the site in 2020.Who sold the property to Zuckerberg and ChanThe sellers were reportedly celebrity cosmetic surgeon Dr Aaron Rollins and his wife, Marine Rollins, a real estate agent. According to the Wall Street Journal, they paid more than $30 million for the approximately two-acre plot in 2020. The couple subsequently spent years developing the property and overseeing the construction of the mansion. It was first listed for sale in November 2025, with an asking price of $200 million. The eventual $170 million transaction was therefore below its original listing price.Where the $170 million sale stands among America's biggest property dealsWhile the transaction established a new benchmark for Miami-Dade County, it was not the most expensive residential property purchase recorded in the United States. That distinction remained with billionaire investor Ken Griffin, who paid approximately $238 million for a New York apartment in 2019. The Indian Creek purchase nevertheless ranks among the country's most expensive residential transactions. It also comes amid increased interest in Florida's high-end property market.The Wall Street Journal also reported that local real estate agents had linked some of the increased demand for luxury properties in Florida to California's proposed billionaire wealth tax. The measure, known as Proposition 40, sought to impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of California residents worth more than $1 billion. However, California voters rejected the proposal in November 2026, meaning it did not become law. Florida, meanwhile, does not impose a state personal income tax.Zuckerberg and Chan's expanding property portfolioThe Miami mansion is another addition to a property portfolio that already includes homes in several parts of the United States. The couple have residential properties in Palo Alto, California, around Lake Tahoe and in Hawaii. Their Hawaiian property has previously attracted attention because of reports about a large compound and underground facilities. Their residential holdings in Palo Alto have also been the subject of coverage, with reports detailing multiple home purchases over the years.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports and property records. The Times of India has not independently verified the property's specifications, construction status or planned amenities.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Trump China summit with Putin and Xi high on spectacle
articles.summary: The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summit.
articles.body:
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and it appears that he left with little in return.

In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as an historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.

The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.

Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting

This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls

In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success.

That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.

So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.

While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.

On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.

For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique , released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".

That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.

"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.

A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.

If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.

While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.

But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.

"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.

"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."

Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.

"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.

Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.

In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.

Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

articles.title: China could exploit US technology to threaten American forces, congressional watchdog leaders warn
articles.summary: China could gain access to American chips and AI infrastructure without companies’ knowledge, congressional watchdog leaders warn, potentially advancing weapons that threaten U.S. forces.
articles.body: China's military could exploit advanced American technology, including through espionage and unauthorized access to artificial intelligence infrastructure, to develop weapons that could ultimately threaten U.S. forces, two congressional China watchdog leaders warned in an interview with Fox News Digital. The officials raised concerns that Beijing is seeking to acquire sophisticated U.S. semiconductors and access powerful AI data centers, potentially strengthening its military capabilities without the knowledge or involvement of the American companies behind the technology. Those concerns are underscored by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission's 2026 annual report, which says Beijing is seeking to circumvent American export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors for military modernization. BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN Citing an April 2026 assessment by Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, the commission reported that China's People's Liberation Army was soliciting advanced Nvidia chips for AI-enabled military capabilities. The report describes Beijing's push toward "intelligentized warfare," integrating AI into weapons systems, targeting, military command and logistics. Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, warned that the threat extends beyond chip exports to access to computing infrastructure abroad. "Anytime the Chinese gain access to advanced chips, we are helping them," Kuiken told Fox News Digital. Commission Chairman Randall Schriver acknowledged the risk, pointing to permitted sales of dual-use technology, inadequate cybersecurity protections and American investments. "I think we need sort of a comprehensive look at how the Americans are either wittingly or unwittingly contributing to Chinese military modernization," Schriver said. Kuiken warned that Chinese AI developers or military institutions could also gain access to powerful data centers. "If we're doing it knowingly, we need to bring it to an end," he said. TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT The warnings come amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's relationship with China. Reuters reported Nov. 18, 2026, that Nvidia had stopped shipping licensed Hopper-generation AI data center chips to Chinese customers, according to interim CEO Colette Kress. The findings also come amid a separate controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned in November following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities have suspected of having intelligence ties to Beijing. Jensen Huang has denied knowing about her alleged intelligence connections, while Beijing has rejected the espionage accusations. Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation. U.S. authorities have not conclusively established that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing, and Fox News Digital could not independently verify the allegations. The commissioners also warned that China's advances extend beyond acquiring American hardware. "Denial and deception is part of the CCP's standing doctrine, and that extends to the PLA, so I'm sure there are things we have yet to discover," Schriver said. FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL He pointed to China's growing use of AI-enabled military systems, including autonomous unmanned platforms. Kuiken warned that Beijing is increasingly integrating advanced AI into existing military technology. "We are absolutely seeing the PLA take the technologies that they have on the shelf today and figuring out how they can deploy the most advanced artificial intelligence capabilities into that ecosystem so that they can gain advantage," he said. Against those concerns, China's Foreign Ministry struck a more cooperative tone regarding AI security in a Nov. 19, 2026, statement following a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Shenzhen. CHINA WATCHDOG WARNS TRUMP FACES ‘2-ON-1’ SHOWDOWN WITH XI, PUTIN AS TAIWAN RISKS MOUNT "China and the United States should strengthen communication and coordination, prevent the security risks of AI, and ensure that AI is always under human control," the ministry said in its account of Xi's remarks. The commission also identifies protecting American data as a leading national security priority, warning that AI could make it easier to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities and compromise sensitive information, amid a series of high-profile technology outages affecting major U.S. companies and government systems. Asked about the recent disruptions involving the NSA, Apple and Chase Bank, Kuiken warned that increasingly sophisticated AI models are making it easier to identify cybersecurity weaknesses. "These frontier models are incredibly good at cyber, which means they're good at coding and coding means it's very easy to find vulnerabilities in things," Kuiken told Fox News Digital. "You're basically seeing these leading organizations around the world do everything they can to lock down their organizations to make sure they're not vulnerable." Kuiken emphasized that the commission's leading recommendation this year focuses on protecting American data, describing it as both a national security priority and an economic resource. "One, we want to protect it to keep ourselves secure and two, we wanna deploy it in the models that we have with the democratic world, controls to get economic benefit from it," he said. The commissioners did not establish any connection between the recent technology outages and Chinese cyber operations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended Beijing's technological development and criticized U.S. export restrictions. "China’s sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation," the spokesperson said. "China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues, opposes abuse of export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serve no one’s interests." "China and the U.S. need to work together to deliver on the important common understandings between the two presidents and uphold the momentum of steady development of China-U.S. economic and trade ties," the spokesperson added. The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton accuses Trump of 'aiding and abetting' humanitarian crisis in Ukraine
articles.summary: Hillary Clinton says President Donald Trump appears to be "aiding and abetting" a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine, in a scathing New York Times op-ed.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Thursday said President Donald Trump appears to be "aiding and abetting" a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine, in a scathing New York Times op-ed. The 2016 Democratic nominee for president penned a New York Times opinion piece headlined, "What Trump Should Have Said to Putin," that criticized Trump’s Thursday trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The White House issued a "U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace," which states that the three leaders intend to communicate on decreasing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear weapons proliferation – but Clinton isn’t satisfied. "A strong, strategic American president should have demanded that the Russian military stop bombarding Ukrainian civilians and destroying their energy and water infrastructure," Clinton wrote. TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE "He should have warned Mr. Xi that China will pay a price for providing support for Russia’s war machine," Clinton continued. "And he should have made it clear to Mr. Putin that his efforts to freeze the Ukrainian people into submission this winter will fail — because the Ukrainians are tougher than Mr. Putin thinks and because the United States and our NATO allies will redouble support to them." Clinton then declared, "No one expected Mr. Trump to do any of this. Initial reports suggest that he didn’t." Clinton accused Trump of making "excuses for Russia" when he said Putin could be even tougher on Ukraine. "Over recent months, the United States has actually reduced its support for Ukraine," Clinton wrote, pointing to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claims about disrupted Starshield access. UKRAINE'S STARLINK RESTORED AS ELON MUSK CLAIMS KYIV VIOLATED TERMS OF SERVICE 'TO KILL PEOPLE' "The administration’s actions have emboldened the Russian dictator, making it less likely that he will make concessions for peace, and have undermined Ukraine’s ability to defend itself," Clinton wrote. "In January, new Democratic majorities in Congress should investigate Mr. Trump’s appeasement of Russia and pressure him to provide more support to Ukraine," she continued. "But the people of Ukraine can’t wait that long." Clinton wrote, "Ukrainian cities will be left without heat or power" this winter and Putin’s "apparent goal is to put millions of people at risk of freezing to death and to create a surge of refugees into the rest of Europe," before calling on "the current lame-duck Congress" to push Trump to help. Clinton ended her opinion piece by declaring, "In January, the new Congress should go further and pass additional support for Ukraine to help it win this war. This is a time for action, not appeasement." TRUMP IS TRYING ‘THE ART OF THE DEAL’ IN UKRAINE BUT WHAT MUST PUTIN GIVE UP? The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Heritage Action media fellow Tim Young mocked "one of the architects of the Russian hoax" for weighing in on what the president should have said to Putin. "Every time I see Hillary Clinton say something like what the president ‘should do,’ I’m reminded of her social media post saying, ‘happy birthday’ to a future president with a picture of a younger her," Young told Fox News Digital. "It just shows she’s jealous she’s not there." Young also suggested that Clinton’s comments prove "it’s not only Republicans who learned nothing from the midterms." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "What is clear from her comments is that she is pro-forever war with Ukraine and Russia, and wars are the opposite of what the American people want," Young said. articles.title: Charges dismissed against boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. over bad check in Las Vegas
articles.summary: LAS VEGAS — A Las Vegas court dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr.
articles.body: LAS VEGAS — A Las Vegas court dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. on Wednesday at the request of prosecutors, following allegations the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch, according to court records. The dismissal came after the watch was returned to the owner, said Clark County District Attorney’s Office spokesperson Andryanna Sheppard. “Both parties are satisfied,” Sheppard said. A hearing in the case that had been scheduled for Thursday was canceled. Mayweather, 49, was charged in April with theft and passing a check without sufficient funds with intent to defraud. Prosecutors in Clark County had alleged Mayweather wrote the $200,000 check to the Las Vegas designer resale store Gold and Beyond in December 2024 despite having insufficient funds in his account, according to the criminal complaint. The Associated Press left emails, voice and text messages seeking comment from Mayweather’s attorney and an attorney for Gold and Beyond. Mayweather, a former five-division world champion, announced his retirement in 2017 with a 50-0 record. After saying earlier this year that he was coming out of retirement, he was scheduled to be in Athens, Greece, for the “Battle of the Legends” boxing match in June. The event was canceled due to a legal dispute with CSI Sports. CSI sued Mayweather in the Southern District of New York district court alleging breach of contract for allegedly failing to fight Mike Tyson in a separate event. Mayweather denied the allegations in court documents. Earlier this year, Mayweather was sued in New York over his alleged failure to pay rent at a Manhattan apartment and was in financial disputes with multiple jewelers. He also filed a lawsuit in New York against his former business manager, alleging a yearslong fraud scheme.

articles.title: Deadly crashes spark safety push at famed beach destination after 5 killed in 2026
articles.summary: Safety concerns accelerated after video captured a hang-gliding instructor and tourist crashing into a wall in Rio de Janeiro, prompting São Conrado's temporary flight suspension.
articles.body: A string of deadly hang-gliding and paragliding crashes has prompted a temporary flight suspension in a popular area of Rio de Janeiro after five people, including an American tourist, died this year. São Conrado, a neighborhood at the center of Rio de Janeiro's hang-gliding and paragliding scene, temporarily suspended air sports Nov. 2, according to a recent Reuters report. The suspension comes after five people, including two tourists, two guides and an army colonel, died in 2026 alone. TOURIST DANGLES 23 STORIES ABOVE STREET IN ‘RECKLESS’ DAREDEVIL STUNT The most recent victims included hang-gliding instructor Luiz Eduardo Rodrigues dos Santos, 45, and 26-year-old passenger Adrian Guillermo Arismendi, of Argentina, on Nov. 2, leading to the recent suspension. Their crash was captured on video as they banked sharply and crashed into a wall near a landing spot. In February, hang-gliding instructor Rodolfo Pascoal Ladeira and 37-year-old American tourist Jenny Colon Rodriguez of North Carolina both died after plunging into the water. In August, an army colonel died after his paraglider also crashed into the water. US TRAVELERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY RIDES AND SEXUAL ASSAULTS TIED TO BEACH VENDORS Now, flight operators and lawmakers are reconsidering how the high-risk sport is regulated. Bruno Menescal, president of the São Conrado Free Flight Club, told Reuters his club "has very strict rules regarding security requirements." TEEN DIES AFTER FALLING FROM MOVING CARNIVAL RIDE AS QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER SAFETY "Now, more measures will be taken, without doubt," he said. "Now, more measures will be taken, without doubt." There are still rules in place that are apparently routinely stretched. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER For example, Brazil's federal aviation regulator allows two-person flights strictly for instructional purposes, an exception pilots regularly use to take tourists on one-off tandem rides. Menescal added that federal aviation regulators need more staff and enforcement resources to ensure existing rules are followed. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "The dream of flying has been with man ever since man has been on the earth. It goes back to Icarus," Menescal said. "So, we have people who want to [take] their first flight. How are people going to get into the sport if not via an instruction flight?" Accidents involving air sports across Rio had been climbing prior to this year, rising from 43 in 2023 to 44 in 2024 and 56 in 2025, according to Rio's firefighting service. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ While total accidents dropped to 28 so far in 2026, local officials attribute that decline to bad weather, which reduced the number of flights. The firefighting service said 2026's five deaths follow a similar number in 2025, after only one fatality was reported over the previous four years. Meanwhile, former Brazilian soccer star Romário, now a senator in Brazil's Congress, introduced legislation earlier this year to tighten controls on high-risk sports after a woman's death in a bungee-jumping accident. articles.title: Michigan AD's first move should be to fire Kyle Whittingham and write a $24 million buyout check: Trey Wallace
articles.summary: Michigan spent $40 million on its roster and paid Jason Beck nearly $10 million to leave, as questions swirl over Kyle Whittingham's future in 2027.
articles.body: Is it time for Michigan to pull the plug on the Kyle Whittingham experiment after just one season? That’s the question looming in Ann Arbor after the school hired Texas A&M athletic director Trev Alberts to the same position this week. Known for his business decisions over the past few years at both Nebraska and in College Station, Alberts is being brought in to right the Wolverines ship, which could include a decision as to whether Kyle Whittingham is the right man to lead Michigan into 2027. MICHIGAN HIRED KYLE WHITTINGHAM TO FIX ITS MESS. INSTEAD, HE’S CREATED AN EVEN BIGGER ONE WITH WOLVERINES At 5-5, the Wolverines have given fans little to get excited about. What was supposed to be a season of stability has instead delivered expensive mistakes, frustrating football and a series of cringeworthy moments from the head coach. Trev Alberts hired to clean up Wolverine mistakes, and football program When outgoing athletic director Warde Manuel hired Whittingham following the Sherrone Moore debacle, the expectation was straightforward: Stabilize the program and win football games. Nearly eleven months later, Michigan fans are wondering how Moore managed a better record in 2025 than Whittingham has delivered in 2026 with such an expensive football team. With two regular-season games remaining, including the showdown with Ohio State after playing No. 4 UCLA this weekend, those questions aren’t going away. It probably doesn’t help that Michigan spent upward of $40 million on this roster, which included a lucrative deal for quarterback Bryce Underwood that is currently being wasted after losing the starting job. Oh, and Michigan will assuredly have to overpay for players this transfer portal season thanks to a disappointing 2026. Sure, the right price goes a long way, but these athletes would also like to compete for a championship. So, the Wolverines could be put in a spot where paying 30% more for a player is the only way to get them to sign, if Whittingham returns in 2027 with the same structure. Oh, and the Wolverines also fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck after just ten games into the season. BIG MONEY, BIGGER DISASTER: MINNESOTA EXPOSES MICHIGAN AS WOLVERINES ARE LATEST EXAMPLE OF WASTED NIL FUNDS Did I mention that Michigan is also having to pay former offensive coordinator Jason Beck nearly $10 million to leave, thanks to his buyout? Simply put, this has been a disaster for the Michigan football program. And no, it doesn’t feel as though it's going to get any better over the next year. So when Michigan decided that Trev Alberts was the right man for the athletic director position, the conversations quickly shifted as to whether Whittingham would return in 2027. Wolverines have to make a tough decision on Kyle Whittingham During his interview process with the school, multiple sources told OutKick that Michigan made it clear that it wanted Alberts to conduct an internal review of the football program that included what steps needed to be taken to ensure a profitable future. That's not good news for Whittingham, unless you're handling his financial accounts. After signing a five-year deal that includes around a $24 million buyout if fired without cause, the Michigan head coach is sitting in a comfortable position in terms of his checking account. FLORIDA STATE FIRES MIKE NORVELL AFTER FAN REVOLT, CLEMSON LOSS SPARK DECISION TO PAY MASSIVE BUYOUT But, that doesn’t mean he's fine with having his legacy take a hit based off one season in Ann Arbor. Unfortunately for Whittingham, that will not be his decision. If Michigan feels as though Trev Alberts can put together a plan that will get the Wolverines back on track with a potential new head coach, which would be the fourth in six years, the school might need to just pay the buyout and start over. His first season at Michigan has already led to questions about whether he would like to remain the head coach in 2027, amid this abysmal situation. "Yeah. But I guess anything I say, you can say, ‘Oh, that means he wants to get fired.’ To me, that’s ridiculous," Whittingham responded. "Do I want to continue? Yes sir, I would like to continue. … That might be the most bizarre thing I’ve heard there." "I don't know who spun it that way, but like I said, you can take anything and spin it any way you want and try to get the desired outcome you're looking for. That was not the intention." MICHIGAN LOSES AGAIN AND THE NOISE AROUND KYLE WHITTINGHAM'S JOB GROWS AS OREGON KEEPS PLAYOFF HOPES ALIVE There are plenty of coaches in college football that would take the Michigan job, and certainly understand what it entails during this period of transition in Ann Arbor. Are we about to have that sort of conversation, again? If Kyle Whittingham loses to both UCLA and Ohio State over the next two weeks, that call could be made for him. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But, this is the reason why Trev Alberts was hired to lead the Michigan athletic department. It might be an expensive decision, but the Wolverines don't have time to sit around and wait for Whittingham to figure out how to right the Michigan ship.

articles.title: Iran regime's execution spree continues as twins face death penalty, decades in prison after alleged torture
articles.summary: Two Iranian twin sisters allege the judge hearing their torture complaint was the official who assaulted them during interrogation, their cousin says.
articles.body: Two Iranian twin sisters imprisoned for participating in anti-government protests came face-to-face with the very official they accused of torturing and sexually assaulting them when they appeared in court to seek justice. They discovered he was the judge assigned to hear their complaint, their U.S.-based cousin told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. Masoud Nourmohammadi, the cousin of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, alleged that the official had been involved in their interrogation and subsequently presided over the complaint they filed against the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). "As soon as they walk in, they see the exact person who tortured them and sexually assaulted them is the judge," Nourmohammadi said. IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS; THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN He claimed the complaint was immediately dismissed by that same official. "The judge was their prosecutor during the building (of) the case, and he was the one that did the sexual assault on the kids and tortured them as a prosecutor and for the lawsuit he was assigned as a judge for that lawsuit," Nourmohammadi said. Fox News Digital has not independently verified the allegations or reviewed the court documents. The twins, now 21, were arrested after January anti-government demonstrations in Isfahan. According to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), Taraneh was sentenced to death and an additional 11 years in prison, while Romina received a 36-year prison sentence. The sentences were issued in the so-called Shohada Square case involving 16 defendants. IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST Nourmohammadi said the sisters' legal situation has become increasingly precarious. One of their attorneys has been arrested, another withdrew from the case and the family has since secured a new lawyer to pursue the appeal of the criminal verdict. He also described alarming new reports about their health. "We just heard from another inmate who was with them in the same prison that the girls have been throwing up, vomiting blood in the night," Nourmohammadi said. He claimed Taraneh had previously been unable to walk after allegedly being tortured and that both sisters were being denied necessary medical treatment. Their case comes amid growing international concern over Iran's use of the death penalty against people arrested during nationwide anti-government demonstrations. IRANIAN PROTESTER HANGED HOURS AFTER MARRYING HIS IMPRISONED FIANCÉE OVER JAIL PHONE LINE A Nov. 16 report by Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) documented at least 121 protest-related death sentence cases after January's demonstrations, including six women and at least five people who were minors at the time of their alleged offenses. The organization cautioned that some sentences had subsequently been overturned or referred for retrial. According to IHRNGO, 41 protesters have been executed since March 18, including 39 connected to January's protests and two linked to the earlier Woman, Life, Freedom movement. "Despite the execution of more than one protester every week on average since March, the international response has failed to raise the political cost of these executions sufficiently to deter the Islamic Republic," IHRNGO Director Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam said. The warning coincided with the U.N. General Assembly's Third Committee adopting a resolution Wednesday condemning Tehran's human rights record, with 76 countries voting in favor, 27 against and 64 abstaining. UN WATCHDOG SLAMS POTENTIAL ELECTION OF IRAN TO PANEL WITH HUMAN RIGHTS SWAY: 'LUNATICS RUNNING THE ASYLUM' Explaining the U.S. vote, Ambassador Dan Negrea said Washington believed the text did not go far enough in holding the Iranian government accountable and contained language that distracted from its central purpose. "Let no one mistake our abstention for any softening toward Tehran," Negrea said. "For 47 years, the regime has ruled through torture and terror. It crushes dissent with public executions and beatings. It remains the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism, and its repression does not stop at its own borders. It pursues those who dare to speak up against it and hunts them down around the world. "Today, it unjustly executes more people than any other country. The United Nations has documented these human rights violations and abuses at length, and responsibility for them belongs to the regime alone." Iran's U.N. mission rejected the resolution, accusing its sponsors of politicizing human rights and ignoring the consequences of sanctions and military conflict. Nourmohammadi, who lives in Utah, said he has contacted congressional representatives seeking help but has not received a response. He said Tehran uses executions to intimidate Iranians considering further demonstrations. "That's one of the reasons that the Islamic Republic is executing people is just to create that fear," he said. articles.title: An Illinois mother was killed in 1966 as her two-month-old daughter slept nearby; nearly 60 years later, a family friend who carried her coffin has been convicted of the murder after DNA revived the case
articles.summary: In November 1966, 18-year-old Karen Snider was at her home in Calumet City, Illinois, with her two-month-old daughter when a family friend came to visit.
articles.body: In November 1966, 18-year-old Karen Snider was at her home in Calumet City, Illinois, with her two-month-old daughter when a family friend came to visit. Her husband, Paul Snider, was at work. The baby was sleeping nearby when Karen was stabbed more than 120 times.The murder remained unsolved for nearly six decades. Now, James Barbier, the man who was once a friend of the couple and helped carry Karen's coffin at her funeral, has been convicted of her murder. He was 81 when a jury found him guilty of first-degree murder on November 9, 2026.As reported by PEOPLE, the conviction followed a renewed investigation in which DNA testing of evidence from the crime scene helped identify Barbier as a suspect. He had been arrested shortly after the killing in 1966 but was never charged at the time.A family friend who knew when her husband was awayKaren was killed on November 12, 1966, while her husband was working at the Indiana Harbor Belt Railroad. Their daughter, Paula, was just two months old. During the trial, Cook County Assistant State's Attorney Krystyn Dilillo said Barbier was friends with both Karen and Paul and worked with her husband. He also knew Paul's work schedule.According to the prosecution, Karen allowed Barbier into the house because she knew him. He then attacked her with a weapon, stabbing her 125 times, including in the neck and chest. The injuries also affected her heart, liver and lungs. The autopsy showed defensive wounds on Karen's hands, indicating that she had tried to resist the attack.Her husband returned from work at around 11 pm and found her dead in their home. Their infant daughter had been sleeping in her bassinet nearby. In her closing arguments, Dilillo described how Karen had let someone she considered a friend into her home. "She put up a fight. She tried to save her life," the prosecutor said, according to PEOPLE. "But she lost that fight. He won."Why police suspected him but did not charge himInvestigators had limited evidence when the murder took place. According to reports, police found blood spatter near a broken basement window. Barbier came under suspicion soon after the killing. His wife reportedly told investigators that he returned home that night appearing nervous, with cuts and blood on him. She also said he put his clothes straight into the washing machine, which was unusual for him. People at Karen's funeral also noticed cuts on Barbier, according to the prosecution's account.He was arrested in 1966 but was not charged. He even served as a pallbearer at Karen's funeral, helping carry the coffin of the woman he would eventually be convicted of murdering. The case remained cold for decades, with no one held responsible for Karen's death.A tip in 2022 brought the case back to investigatorsThe investigation took a new direction in 2022, when a man named Kevin Seeley contacted police. As reported by The Sun, he remembered his grandmother talking about the murder and decided to pass the information to investigators.Detectives reopened the case and returned to evidence preserved from the original crime scene. New DNA testing helped link Barbier to the killing. As reported by The Independent in May 2024, investigators had obtained DNA matches involving blood stains on Barbier's trousers and Karen's dress. The renewed forensic work gave authorities grounds to pursue the case again.Barbier, who had moved to Missouri, was arrested at his home in Creve Coeur in 2024. He was eventually tried and convicted by a jury in November 2026.Daughter waited nearly 60 years for an answerPaula Larson was only two months old when her mother was killed. She grew up without Karen and later learnt about the circumstances of her death from her father, who died in 1989. Following the verdict, Larson spoke about the long wait for accountability. She told PEOPLE that she hoped Barbier would never be released from prison.She also expressed relief that the conviction came before more members of the family died. Barbier is scheduled to be sentenced on December 15, 2026.The conviction closes a criminal case that had remained unresolved since 1966. For Karen's daughter, it also brings a long-awaited answer about the man who killed her mother and was present at her funeral.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Photos: Genocide ruling spotlights human toll of 2017 Rohingya crisis
articles.summary: Nearly a million Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in 2017, forming one of the world’s largest refugee camps near Cox’s Bazar.
articles.body:
The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, finding the military acted with “genocidal intent” and killed about 10,000 people during its 2017 operations in Rakhine state.

In a landmark judgement under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar in breach of its obligations — a decision Rohingya activists hope will finally bring accountability for years of mass killings, rapes and the burning of villages.

Nearly a million Rohingya fled those attacks, crossing into Bangladesh and building one of the world’s largest refugee settlements around Cox’s Bazar.

Today, many remain confined to overcrowded, fragile camps, stateless and with little prospect of safe return, even as the ICJ ruling sharpens pressure on Myanmar’s military and raises wider questions about justice for victims of mass atrocities.

This photo story returns to the early months of the crisis in 2017, documenting Rohingya families arriving exhausted and traumatised, queuing for food and trying to rebuild a semblance of community in the makeshift camps.

Through these images, all captured in September 2017, we see how the violence now recognised as genocide reshaped countless lives – and why, for Rohingya still living in limbo, the court’s judgement is only one step in a much longer struggle for safety, rights and a home.

images.caption: Rohingya refugee women with their children stand in line outside a food distribution centre at Balukhali refugee camp, about 50km (32 miles) from Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2017, after fleeing Myanmar. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]

Rohingya refugees arrive in Bangladesh, carrying the few possessions they managed to take during a last-minute escape from Myanmar soldiers who attacked their village, killing and raping residents and burning their homes. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]

A Rohingya girl and her mother rest by the roadside after crossing the Bangladesh–Myanmar border, exhausted from days of walking along muddy tracks while carrying the few belongings they could salvage from their village. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Excise dept approaches NIC seeking new transfer-scoring formula ahead of polls
articles.summary: Uttar Pradesh excise department asks NIC to revise Manav Sampada transfer scoring ahead of polls, seeking more weight for merit over hardship criteria.
articles.body: Lucknow: Taking a different stand, the excise department has approached the National Informatics Centre (NIC) to rework the formula used to calculate the scores of officials due to be transferred through the Manav Sampada portal. Adhering to the guidelines of the Election Commission, state govt has set a deadline of Nov 30 to identify and shift officers holding key positions away from the district if they have already spent three or more years of service there as of May 31, 2027, ahead of the elections. As a result, heads of more than 75 govt agencies have started shortlisting the names of officials who have remained posted in the same district since May 30, 2024. As the EC has this time made it binding on the state to transfer officials who have served in the same constituency/district during the previous Lok Sabha elections (2024), assembly elections (2022) and by-elections, an exhaustive exercise is needed to go through the service sheet of every officer individually. As per the stipulated rules, about 40% of the 584 excise inspectors could be transferred from their current postings. Similarly, up to 30% of the 137 excise sub-inspectors could also be shuffled. With such large-scale movement of officials in the offing, questions have been raised over the scoring system to be followed during online transfers, as per a govt order issued by the then chief secretary on Aug 3, 2023. “Greater weightage is being given to personal hardships than performance, capabilities and functional requirements in the present scenario. Ideally, credibility, integrity and annual appraisal scores of an officer shall be given the highest value in the scoring order. But medical reasons, posting of spouse (only govt service), personal hardships are accorded higher values than the merit,” said an officer opposing the present criteria. Taking note of the reservations of officials, who act as the backbone of the department in the field for revenue collection and enforcement, the excise department has approached NIC to suggest a reworked scoring formula by Nov 25, a source said. The GO gives department heads the option to allocate the highest score to the functional capabilities of an officer as per rule. “The department has approached NIC to suggest a formula which also gives considerable weightage to proven capabilities of an officer. Or we can do away with some grounds mentioned in the GO while finalising the score. The final call is yet to be taken on the matter,” said an officer. Officials also pointed out that several departments responsible for revenue generation as well as enforcement, such as state tax, mining and transport, are carrying out the transfer procedure ahead of the elections offline instead of adhering to the govt order. articles.title: A Philadelphia teacher was fired after refusing weekly Covid tests, but not one elected school board member attended his termination hearing; five years later, Pennsylvania's top court upheld a ruling in his favour
articles.summary: A Philadelphia teacher who lost his job after refusing to undergo weekly Covid-19 tests has won a legal battle that began during the pandemic.
articles.body: A Philadelphia teacher who lost his job after refusing to undergo weekly Covid-19 tests has won a legal battle that began during the pandemic. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has ruled in his favour, finding that the school district violated state law by holding his termination hearing without a single elected school board member present.The ruling, delivered on November 17, concerns Neal Follman, a teacher in the School District of Philadelphia. The court upheld an earlier decision ordering the district to reinstate him with back pay unless it properly terminates his employment in accordance with the law.The case turned on a question of procedure: can a school board delegate a tenured teacher's dismissal hearing entirely to an appointed hearing officer, then decide the teacher's fate by reviewing the record afterwards? The state's highest court said no.Why the teacher refused Covid testingAccording to the Pennsylvania Department of Education's official record, Follman was employed by the Philadelphia School District from January 2010 and worked at Constitution High School during the 2020-21 school year.On February 22, 2021, the district's then superintendent, William Hite, informed staff that employees returning to schools for in-person learning would have to undergo weekly Covid-19 testing. The testing was to be carried out by medical providers at school premises during working hours. Employees could seek an exemption on medical grounds.Follman submitted a refusal and exemption request on May 7, 2021. He listed concerns including the test's emergency-use authorisation, its accuracy, the handling of testing materials and the company administering the tests. However, he did not complete the section of the form asking him to provide a justification for a medical exemption.The district told him that his reasons were insufficient and warned that disciplinary action would follow if he continued to refuse testing. Follman maintained his refusal. His school principal, Brianna Dunn-Robb, recommended his termination. A district hearing officer also recommended that he be dismissed and suspended without pay while the decision was pending.The school board initially adopted a resolution supporting the termination recommendation in August 2021. Follman was then issued a statement of charges and given the opportunity to challenge the proposed dismissal.The termination hearing that no elected board member attendedFollman chose to contest the proposed termination through a hearing under Pennsylvania's Local Agency Law. The hearing was initially scheduled for September 13, 2021, but was postponed. The district later decided to hold it virtually, despite objections from Follman and his lawyer, who had sought an in-person hearing.The hearing eventually took place by videoconference in February 2022. No elected member of the Philadelphia Board of Education attended. Instead, the board appointed a hearing officer, Rudolph Garcia, to preside over the proceedings. Follman challenged the arrangement, arguing that Pennsylvania's Public School Code required him to be heard before the elected school board directors themselves.On August 18, 2022, the board voted 9-0 to dismiss him. It adopted the hearing officer's findings and conclusions. The Pennsylvania Department of Education's Secretary of Education initially upheld the dismissal. The secretary reasoned that the board could appoint a hearing officer as long as its members reviewed the findings and made an independent decision based on the record. Follman appealed.What the courts saidIn July 2024, the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania reversed the secretary's decision. It held that the school board had not complied with the statutory procedure for dismissing a tenured teacher. The court ordered Follman's reinstatement with back pay unless the district properly terminated his employment.The Philadelphia School District challenged that decision before the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. It argued that the Public School Code allowed school boards to delegate the task of conducting termination hearings to appointed hearing officers. In its November 17, 2026 ruling, the Supreme Court rejected that argument.Justice David Wecht, writing for the majority, referred to Section 1127 of the Pennsylvania Public School Code. The provision says that a school board must conduct a hearing before dismissing a tenured professional employee and give that employee an opportunity to be heard "before the board of school directors".The court interpreted this to mean that at least some elected board members must be present. It held that a hearing conducted with no elected directors in attendance could not be considered a hearing before the board.The judgment stated: "For present purposes, it suffices to say that a hearing with no school directors in attendance is not a hearing 'before the board of school directors.'"The court also pointed to Section 1129, which requires the board to consider the charges and testimony before voting on a dismissal. It rejected the district's argument that members could simply review the hearing officer's findings and vote afterwards.Importantly, the Supreme Court did not specify exactly how many board members must attend such hearings. It said that deciding whether a quorum or a smaller number is sufficient was outside the scope of this case. The question before it was whether all elected directors could stay away. The court's answer was no.The ruling affirmed the Commonwealth Court's decision reinstating Follman with back pay, unless and until the district carries out a lawful termination.What the ruling does and does not decideThe case was not a judgment that Follman's refusal to undergo Covid testing was justified. The Supreme Court's decision focused on whether the school district followed the procedure required by law when it dismissed a tenured teacher.The original termination decision had relied on allegations of persistent negligence and wilful neglect of duties. The Secretary of Education had accepted the district's grounds for dismissal, but the later court proceedings found that the absence of elected board members at the hearing made the termination process legally defective.The ruling therefore centres on the rights of tenured public-school teachers facing dismissal in Pennsylvania. It makes clear that a school board cannot avoid its statutory responsibility by allowing an appointed hearing officer to conduct the entire hearing while every elected director remains absent.You use AI every day.
